orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No gate is named. Target orders descend from gates D and V: WO-053's first external change and WO-112's scratch-target loop, which the capability rows show as demonstrated. WO-291 hardens that path for every later target order; it does not unblock an open gate. The Cost line places the recurring amendment with 'an instance's operator', so the beneficiaries are instances' target orders. WO-083's title does not say whether its Angular order is a target order, so a link to gate P is possible but not shown. NoOp cost in the records: the WO-291 cost-table row has null metrics, and the evidence is stale. The removal the order claims (one operator-authorized amendment each time a pin goes stale, and a hand edit of each target heading) is not counted in any supplied observation. Its size is unknown.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the new fetch is bounded by a row of the time-limits table and is never a stop, so it cannot add guard refusals. The changed-bytes refusal is kept, but its message now names both ways to repair (criterion 8), which should reduce retries. Tragedy of the commons: one bounded network fetch per target start, with its time measured on core's host before and after. Accounted for. Drift to low performance: no root text is named. Neutral. Escalation: modest. Readers must handle two line forms (pinned and unpinned) for good, and two records hold the base: the activation event and the registry entry. Criterion 2 checks they are equal at the start; nothing guards them from drifting apart later. Success to the successful: pinning stays available, so the credible alternative survives. Shifting the burden: favourable. It removes the operator's recurring amendments for stale pins. Rule beating: criterion 1 row 6 samples two of the programs a clone's configuration can run (finding 1); the other control rows are backed by planted faults. Seeking the wrong goal: aligned. The recorded start commit keeps the exact task state the one-paragraph story asks for, and the fetch fallback keeps the start offline-capable.
orders.removalBalance: Plausibly yes, but not quantified. The addition is mechanism: a fetch, a second admitted line form and the readers that handle it, one advisory and about eleven cases. The removal is operator work that recurs with every stale pin and every target heading. In operator attention the removal recurs per order while the addition is paid once. In code the addition is larger. The Cost line does not count past stale-pin amendments, so calling the removal larger is an inference.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades. If the fetch fails or outlasts its limit, the start uses the remote-tracking base as it stood and prints one advisory with the commit's full id and committer date (criterion 1 rows 2-3; criterion 3). With no origin, it starts from the local base branch. The fetch is never a stop. Activating an unpinned order with no started worktree is a new refusal (criterion 2 row 2), but it replaces the base's blanket refusal of the line and names 'worktree start'. Plan check's changed-bytes refusal already exists and only gains its two routes. A malformed line is still refused, now with both forms named.

findings.reason: Row 6 plants two programs that a clone's configuration can run during a fetch: remote.origin.uploadpack, and a hook under core.hooksPath. Its planted fault is 'the start runs the clone's own git fetch'. It does not sample other programs a clone can configure, such as core.fsmonitor, core.sshCommand, a credential helper, or a url.insteadOf rewrite paired with a protocol allowance. An implementation that neutralizes only the two planted keys would pass while still running code the clone configures. The row implies a guarantee about a whole class (the start runs nothing the clone's configuration names), but its evidence covers two members.
findings.reopenWhen: During 'worktree start' of an unpinned target order, a marker planted through any other key of the clone's local configuration appears.

findings.reason: A moving base changes what the controls mean. With the unpinned line, the commit an order's controls were written against ('fails at the base') is not the commit the order starts from. The activation records the start commit, but nothing records the commit the planner and the refuter judged. If the target's base moves between filing and start, a control row can pass at the recorded start commit, and replaying the judgment cannot recover which base it assumed.
findings.reopenWhen: A target order filed with the unpinned line has a control row that fails at filing time but passes at its recorded start commit, or a verifier cannot state which base a control row was judged against.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No gate is named. Every order uses the drive and main's integration script, so WO-294 is machinery under all the remaining gates, P (WO-083) included, rather than the unblocking of one. NoOp cost in the records: the WO-294 cost-table row has null metrics, and the evidence is stale. The removal the order claims is not counted in any supplied observation. That removal is the operator's switch of the primary checkout back to main for each drive during a planning pass, or running the phases by hand, plus the refused drive, status and integration for an order that adds a configuration key. Unknown, not zero.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: material. Two loaders now judge the same file differently. The strict loader serves a checkout's own commands; a tolerant roots reader serves lookups across checkouts. Criterion 6 and its planted fault keep the strict loader strict, so the two cannot quietly merge. What remains is a semantic risk (finding 1). Tragedy of the commons: no shared compute is consumed, and operator attention is saved on every drive. Drift to low performance: no root text. Neutral. Escalation: one more reader and one more lookup branch. A second path for reading configuration is a surface that later orders must keep consistent. Success to the successful: the compiled text does not weigh a versioned configuration contract, in which main declares the keys it reads and a worktree declares its schema edition. The tolerant reader is the cheaper local fix. Shifting the burden: favourable. It removes the recurring operator rescue of switching checkouts or running phases by hand. Rule beating: criteria 4 and 5 assert a status and a launch, but not where the drive writes its control records when no worktree holds main (finding 2). Seeking the wrong goal: aligned. A drive that starts during a planning pass is a direct gain in operator flow.
orders.removalBalance: Yes in operator attention, but not quantified. The addition is one roots reader, its use at the lookups that cross checkouts, one lookup branch and about six cases. The removal is an operator action on every drive during every planning pass, plus three refusals for any order that adds a configuration key. The records do not count such switches.
orders.failureBehavior: Mostly degrades. Where no control plane is found, the old message stays as the fallback, which the compiled criteria imply rather than test. The strict refusal of an unknown key in a checkout's own configuration is kept on purpose (criterion 6). That is correct, because it guards the checkout's own commands. The remaining risk runs the other way: if the tolerant reader ignores a key that moves a root, it goes on with wrong paths when it should refuse (finding 1).

findings.reason: A roots reader that ignores the keys it does not know is safe only while those keys never change what the known roots mean. Suppose an order adds or renames a key that moves a document or control root. Main's reader would build the old path from the keys it knows and then integrate, read status or write at the wrong root without refusing, while the worktree's own strict loader would build the new path. The criteria plant only keys that leave the roots alone.
findings.reopenWhen: An order adds or renames a configuration key that changes a root, and main's integrate or status then reads or writes at a path the order worktree's own strict loader does not compute.

findings.reason: When no worktree holds main, criterion 5 asserts only that the fake host receives a launch. It does not assert where the drive records its dispatch and control events when no checkout of main exists: main's control log through some other route, the current branch of the primary checkout, or nowhere. A launch with no control event, or with one written on a branch that is not main, would pass. What is at stake is that the control plane has a single location.
findings.reopenWhen: In a fixture with no main worktree, a launched drive leaves its dispatch or control event somewhere other than main's control log, or leaves none.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No gate is named. The outcome is the mission's: fewer turns that end over a choice the session could make itself. It underlies every remaining gate, P included. NoOp cost in the records: across WO-277 to WO-287 the shifting-the-burden observation shows operator corrections of 8, 4, 1, 5 and 13 and directions of 0, 0, 1, 1 and 4. WO-287's four directions are 3 resumeDirection and 1 resumeAnswer. That fits sessions stopping to be steered, but no row attributes a correction or direction to a turn end, so the NoOp cost is unknown. The WO-289 cost-table row has null metrics. The order's byte figures check out: the drift observation shows the executor at 51,169 against 51,226, the reviewer at 45,310 against 45,385 and the planner at 34,864 against 34,876, that is 57, 75 and 12 bytes under.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: material. In roots where the stops advise, the bound, gate and worker-cap messages say the call went on (criterion 4), and the rule says the work goes on (criterion 5). Criterion 1 lists no bound among the three reasons to end a turn. So in the session's instructions an advising bound no longer bounds anything, and the dispatch's goal and the bound's guard can undo each other (finding 4). Tragedy of the commons: sessions that keep going spend more shared compute and tokens per dispatch. The Cost line counts bytes, not that spend. Drift to low performance: material. Each of six roots gains about three lines while sitting 57, 75 and 12 bytes under its ceiling. CLAUDE.md and the kit template (criterion 9) also count toward every root's cold start. The drift series rises every time (50,410 to 51,169), and the acceptance history raised the executor ceiling from 24,576 to 51,226 in steps of 4,096. The pledge to remove at least what is added pushes back; the no-acceptance handoff leaves breaches advisory (finding 5). Escalation: low. It rewrites text and adds one context line and one reader branch, with no new stop (non-goal). Success to the successful: the compiled text does not ask whether a typed mechanism, the vision's compiled rule, should replace the prose rule rather than rewrite it. WO-290's Stop-hook mechanism is weighed separately. Shifting the burden: favourable. It targets recurring operator re-prompts directly. Rule beating: material. Criteria 1, 2, 5 and 9 check only that text is present (finding 1). Seeking the wrong goal: aligned, with one risk: optimizing for fewer turn ends rather than turn ends at the right moment. The three-reason list guards against that.
orders.removalBalance: Equal in root bytes by pledge, and plausibly larger in operator attention. The order adds about three lines to each of six roots, changes the text of supports, briefings, hooks and a rule, and adds a context line, a reader branch and about twelve cases. It removes the turn-boundary offer before each queued action from every executor dispatch, and the instruction to pause again from every later prompt in analysis. It pledges to remove at least the root bytes it adds. The code and test additions are not offset, and the attention saved is not counted.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades. When the journal or the transcript cannot be read, the context line for a message sent mid-turn is withheld (criterion 8 row 4), which is the old behavior. Advise-level messages report and go on instead of refusing, and no new stop is added (non-goal). If a prompt is misclassified, analysis stays on, which is also the old behavior. At handoff, a root over its ceiling is named and boarded as a follow-up rather than refused.

findings.reason: Rule beating. Criteria 1, 2, 5 and 9 assert that emitted texts hold or omit phrases. None observes a session going on past a choice it can make, or ending a turn only for the three reasons. Every text can pass while sessions keep stopping as before.
findings.reopenWhen: Either of two observations once WO-289 lands. A dispatch's session journal shows Stop rows before the dispatch completes, each followed by an operator prompt, with no operator pause, stop or cancel, no refusal naming the operator, and no task of the session's own pending. Or the operatorDirections series fails to fall over the next orders.

findings.reason: The executor root is left contradicting itself. Criterion 1 makes blocked-turn say a turn ends for three reasons only, and the objective says no text says the opposite. Yet the non-goals leave 'the executor's own sentence on ending a turn' to WO-288. WO-297's non-goals keep 'the executor's other reasons to end a turn', and its criterion 3 requires the clause 'finish the step in hand, write docs/evidence/WO-NNN/standing.md and end the turn'. If any of those other reasons falls outside the three, the executor root says both. No criterion in either order checks the two rules against each other.
findings.reopenWhen: After both WO-297 and WO-289, the emitted dotln-executor root holds a reason to end a turn that is not one of blocked-turn's three.

findings.reason: Criterion 9 says analysis ends 'at a dispatch', but criterion 6 tests only 'resume: next', 'planning:', 'ideation:' and 'drive: WO-NNN'. The lifecycle phases the subject names (repair, verification, final review, release close) are dispatched by their own resume phrases, and none of them is a case. So the reader's branch defines what counts as a dispatch, not the criterion, and a session could end up carrying both the analysis context and a lifecycle dispatch's context.
findings.reopenWhen: A repair, verification, final-review or release-close dispatch prompt sent while analysis is on leaves analysis on, or receives both contexts.

findings.reason: What a bound means in an advising root. With dispatch-bound at advise, criterion 4's message says the call went on and criterion 5's rule says the work goes on, while criterion 1 lists no bound among the reasons to end a turn. A dispatch that never completes is then left with no instruction that ends it. The mission says flow does not silently authorize perpetual action. Because the advisory is not silent, this is a risk, not a contradiction.
findings.reopenWhen: In a root where dispatch-bound advises, a dispatch runs past its bound by more than the bound's own length again without completing, or one dispatch's spend exceeds what the owner set.

findings.reason: Byte accounting. Criterion 9 changes CLAUDE.md and the kit's CLAUDE template, which count toward every role's cold start, including the planner's at 12 bytes under its ceiling. The before-and-after measure in the Cost line names only the six roots, so the pledge to remove at least what is added has to include the shared floor's bytes to hold. Separately, the handoff route (a root over its ceiling is named and boarded, and no acceptance is recorded) departs from the route the supplied acceptances quote, under which a breach is raised to the measured bytes plus 4,096 and is 'never trimmed around or left advisory across orders'. The order cites product 07's Discipline, which the subject does not include.
findings.reopenWhen: Either of two observations: an emitted root exceeds its accepted ceiling after WO-289; or a root is handed off over its ceiling with no acceptance, and the next order's cold-start verdict reports the breach as unaccepted.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No typed gate names it; it applies the unattended outcome that gate R's chain established (work goes on while the operator is away) to dispatched sessions, and serves gate P's drive of an instance's order. NoOp in the records, checked here: WO-288-D168 in the WO-288 worktree records 43 minutes with no task (00:07 to 00:50 UTC) after an executor ended its turn for a decision none of its steps needed; the order calls this the one timed case and says frequency is unmeasured. Without it the operator's prompt remains the only restart for a Claude session that stops early, while the Codex adapter already permits one continuation.
orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: the Stop-hook decision pushes the same way as WO-289's texts and lets the turn end under a background task, a plan awaiting approval, analysis or override, a host continuation already in progress, or an unreadable journal or log, so it neither fights the pause controls nor loops. Tragedy of the commons: one continued turn per early stop, tokens unknown. Drift to low performance: no role root changes; one KIT.md statement. Escalation: a one-time block can provoke a one-line stop written only to satisfy it, and the hook does not read the message (non-goal). Success to the successful: mirrors the Codex adapter's single continuation; no alternative excluded. Shifting the burden to the intervenor: removes the operator's restart prompt. Rule beating: the hook table and the reason are tested, not whether the continued turn did work. Seeking the wrong goal: aimed at idle time, the mission's babysitting cost.
orders.removalBalance: Plausibly yes, unmeasured: one hook decision, one feature and its default, one reason text and about eight cases, plus one continued turn per early stop, against an operator prompt and its idle time per early stop (43 minutes in the one timed case). Frequency is not measured, so the balance is an inference.
orders.failureBehavior: Degrades: the feature off, an unreadable journal or control log, a host-reported continuation, a running background task, a plan awaiting approval, or analysis or override each let the turn end as today, and the second end is always allowed. No tool call is refused and no row is added to the table of stops; an owner turns it off with one election (criterion 3).

findings.reason: The continuation is satisfied either by going on or by a one-line statement of what only the operator can do, and the hook never reads which (non-goal); a session can end its second turn on a block that is not the operator's alone, so the evidence passes without the work.
findings.reopenWhen: A session's one-line end after a continuation names a block that a later dispatch clears without the operator.

orders.systemTraps: Policy resistance: material. Today the refuter's instruction allows a hold only for an observed failure citing an observation id, or for a vision contradiction. A settleability hold is neither. Unless the old instruction is amended, which no criterion requires, the printed prompt will carry two hold standards (finding 1). Tragedy of the commons: every pass adds a fifth answer for each criterion of every judged order (WO-288 alone has 33), so refutation tokens rise by an amount unknown until run. Editing a FEEDBACK_SOURCE_PATHS file also owes one live feedback self-host episode. Drift to low performance: the planner root stands 12 bytes under its ceiling on main and 263 over in WO-288's worktree. The pledge to remove at least what is added is the counterweight; the no-acceptance route is covered in WO-289's finding. Escalation: material. A judge with no tools that holds on a class name alone can produce holds the planner must repair, and the order does not say whether the repair is judged again (finding 2). Success to the successful: the criteria-review helper stays 'for a pass that wants it', so the incumbent practice survives beside the new one (finding 3). Shifting the burden: favourable in intent. It removes later operator adjudication. Rule beating: a defective call needs only a name from DEFECT_CLASSES. Unlike the existing hold kinds, it needs no cited evidence. Seeking the wrong goal: aligned if the side review is actually retired. Otherwise the order adds a judgment without removing one.

One missing answer among dozens then forces the whole refutation to be rerun. No 'unjudged' state is admitted that would file the old four answers with an advisory. Old plan-goal-review-v1 receipts still verify (criterion 4), so existing chains are not refused.

findings.reason: The prompt that 'plan refute' prints today tells the refuter that only an observed failure citing an observation id, or a vision contradiction, holds, and that a constructible counterexample is never a hold. A settleability defect ('no candidate could meet it as written') is judged from the text, without tools, and is neither kind. Criteria 1 and 2 add the question and the schema but do not require that instruction to change, and the non-goals keep 'the four questions the refuter answers now'. The prompt would then state two incompatible hold standards.
findings.reopenWhen: Either of two observations once WO-295 lands: the prompt that 'npm run plan -- refute' prints holds both the observed-failure-or-contradiction rule and the settleability hold; or a refuter declines to hold a defective criterion by citing the older rule.

False holds therefore become planner repairs, and the order does not say whether a repaired criterion is judged again. Either the pass pays for a second judgment, or the planner's repair is filed unjudged.

In a horizon whose judged orders carry dozens of criteria, a single omission forces a full rerun of the one judgment the pass pays for, where the receipt could have been filed with that criterion marked unjudged and an advisory.

orders.criticalPathAndNoOp: No gate is named. Tragedy of the commons: two worker uses per re-cut against the session's cap, tokens unknown, bounded to one re-cut per criterion (criterion 3). Drift to low performance: material. The changed own-decisions rule reaches six roots, four of them over their ceilings in WO-288's worktree. Success to the successful: the other routes (the operator's amendment, the defect record, the waiver) are kept, not displaced. Good. Shifting the burden: favourable, since it removes the operator's adjudication of returned criteria. But undoing a re-cut falls to the operator after the fact (finding 3). Default-on in exported instances lowers that adjudication for owners who never elected it. Row 2 of criterion 6 lets them turn it off, and an unmerged amendment can be undone, so the platform lens is met. Rule beating: material (findings 1 and 2). Seeking the wrong goal: there is a risk that 'the order goes on' becomes the goal in place of 'the order meets its objective'.

Yet the command simply takes 'a planner worker's answer' and 'a refuter's receipt' as inputs, and no criterion checks where they came from. The executing session could write the amended text itself, or get it from a worker it framed, and the command would still bind it.

With a fetch ruled out (a non-goal), the route instead infers 'never pushed' from the absence of a local remote-tracking ref. A branch pushed from another clone, by another tool, or to a remote not named origin has no such ref locally. It would be reported as awaiting-publish, with a command to publish what is already published. The account presents an inference as a fact.
findings.reopenWhen: The route reports awaiting-publish for an order whose branch the origin already holds.

Refusing every fetch is a failure mode whenever a paired pass needs a current main.

For half of every pair, blindness therefore stays held by the role text and the operator, the very state the Removes line claims to remove. findings.reason: The refused forms omit common accidental ways to unblind: git worktree list (which prints sibling worktrees' branches), git rev-list --all, git log --branches or --remotes, git reflog, reading the repository's packed refs, and a Read-tool or cat read of a sibling worktree that holds the other pass. findings.reason: The labels gpt and fable name model families, while the check compares the host the attestation records. The firstVerifications record (5 of the last 8 failed) bears on an order this size (finding).

The measured saving, two order cycles (2.29 full runs and 61 minutes of full gate per closed order, phase medians of 16.9 and 24.8 minutes), compares the merge with splitting it, not with doing nothing. Against NoOp the removals are a rollback by hand that no record shows was needed, a prose-only port whose only new consumer is a fixture, compiled definitions arriving with machinery updates with no recorded harm, and a hand-run upgrade the Cost line itself says was already gone.
